text: Suppose you want a program that guesses the price of a flat from its size. You could try to write the rule yourself, but nobody actually knows the rule. What you do have is a record of flats that have already sold, each with its size and its price. Machine learning is the craft of turning a record like that into a rule, and this whole course is about how that happens.

Draw each sale as a dot, with size along the floor and price up the wall. The dots are scattered, because real prices depend on more than size, yet they clearly drift upward together. A rule that turns a size into a price is what mathematicians call a function: think of a machine with an input slot and an output slot, which for every input hands back exactly one output.

To keep things simple, guess that the rule is a straight line. A line is fixed by two numbers, its slope and the height at which it crosses the wall, so you can think of it as a machine with two knobs. Every setting of the knobs gives a different line, and most of those lines are plainly wrong, because they sail far above or far below the dots.

To say how wrong a line is, measure for every dot the vertical gap between the real price and the price the line predicts. Square each gap, so that misses above and misses below both count against you, and then take the average. That single number is called the loss. It works like a thermometer for wrongness: it reads high when the line is far from the dots, and it falls as the line settles among them.

Learning now has a precise meaning. Start the knobs anywhere, nudge each one in whichever direction makes the loss go down, and repeat until no small nudge helps any more. Watch the line swing round and settle into the cloud of dots. Nobody ever typed the final rule; it was found by searching for the knob settings that fit the data best.

The point of fitting is not the old sales, which you already know, but the next flat that comes along. Because the line captures the trend instead of memorising every dot, you can read off a sensible price for a size the record never contained. That ability to handle new inputs is what we really mean when we say that a model has learned.

A language model is the same idea at an enormous scale. Its input is the text so far, its output is a guess about the next word, and instead of two knobs it has billions, all tuned by the same loop of measuring the loss and nudging. Next, we lay out the map of this course, from the mathematics underneath to the transformer at the top.
